documents: Ao et al. 2022, Geological Journal 57:3251-3266, published paper (PDF)

entry.evidence: Rare systematic geochronology of the Mesozoic strata is reported in the northern Ordos Basin.

steps.action: The authors pose the unsolved question of the source-to-sink relationships of the Mesozoic strata of the northern Ordos Basin, which lacks systematic geochronology.
steps.quote: the determination of the source to sink analysis is technically challenging

steps.action: The authors collect nine outcrop sandstone samples from the Middle Triassic to Lower Cretaceous formations to span the Mesozoic tectonic and sedimentary history (Table 1, Figure 2).
steps.quote: Nine outcrop sandstone samples were collected from upper Triassic, Jurassic, and Lower Cretaceous strata of the northern Ordos Basin

steps.action: The authors separate about 300 zircons per sample, image them by SEM-CL, and date them by LA-ICP-MS U–Pb, keeping ages with <10% discordance.
steps.quote: The U–Pb dating was performed using a Neptune Plus LA-ICP-MS

steps.action: The authors report 715 concordant ages, three dominant age groups (Siderian, Orosirian, Carboniferous), and per-sample KDE peaks and proportions (Figures 3, 4).
steps.quote: Detrital zircon U–Pb geochronology from nine samples yielded 715 concordant ages

steps.action: The authors set five candidate source areas in the Yinshan-Yanshan Orogenic Belt as rival provenances: LS, YS, WLS, DQS and JN.
steps.quote: Five major areas were selected, including the Lang Mts (LS), Yin Mts (YS), Wulas Mts (WLS), Daqing Mts (DQS), Jining (JN)

steps.action: The authors characterize each candidate source's expected age signature from published detrital zircon data (Lei et al. 2017; Figure 5).
steps.quote: The zircon U/Pb ages from the LS in the westernmost area, which cluster at 770–870 Ma

steps.action: The authors compare the sample age spectra with the source-area spectra.
steps.quote: We applied the comparison between the age spectra of the possible source area and study area

steps.action: The authors exclude the Lang Mts as a source because its diagnostic 770–870 Ma group is absent from all samples.
steps.quote: can be easily excluded from being the provenance for the northern Ordos Basin

steps.action: Because the spectra comparison could not separate the remaining sources, the authors switch to cumulative distribution curves and K-S-based MDS.
steps.quote: Therefore, we adopted the cumulative distribution and MDS to study the source-to-sink analysis.

steps.action: The authors compare sample CDF curves (Figure 6) with source CDFs (Figure 5a), assigning JN to YC-1/FX-1/FX-2, WLS to ZL-1 and YS to EM-1, and note the CDF's limits for similar distributions.
steps.quote: confirming the JN area to be the dominant provenance for the northern Ordos Basin

steps.action: The authors analyse the same data with metric MDS of K-S distances (Figure 7), assigning nearest-neighbour sources and recycled sources, and report agreement with the CDF.
steps.quote: the MDS was adopted to distinguish the features of detrital zircons from the sediments and possible source area

steps.action: The authors keep a provenance history with three transfers: YS, then JN, then DQS–WLS, then multiple and recycled sources in the Cretaceous.
steps.quote: provenance was transferred three times during the Mesozoic

steps.action: The authors check the provenance shifts against independent stratigraphic evidence: angular and parallel unconformities at the shift horizons (Figure 2).
steps.quote: further confirmed by the angular unconformity between the Middle Triassic

steps.action: The authors pose the second question: how the basin evolution relates to multiple tectonic regimes.
steps.quote: could provide insights into the relationship between basin evolution and multiple tectonic regimes

steps.action: From the eastward provenance migration, the authors propose that the northern NCC margin was under continuous compression in the Middle–Late Triassic.
steps.quote: we conclude that the northern margin of the NCC experienced continuous

steps.action: The authors take from Cawood et al. (2012) the expected CA-DA cumulative fields for convergent, collisional and extensional basins.
steps.quote: This method uses the crystallization ages (CA) relative to the depositional ages (DA) of the detrital zircons

steps.action: The authors plot the sample CA-DA curves on the Cawood fields (Figure 8), placing EM-1 and YC-1 in the collisional field.
steps.quote: sediments were formed under the collisional setting

steps.action: The authors compare with published regional unconformities, magmatism and deformation across the NCC (Figure 9) that constrain N–S compression.
steps.quote: sequences were developed throughout the NCC

steps.action: The authors list rival drivers of the compression from the literature: closure of the Palaeo-Asian and Mongol-Okhotsk oceans, or North–South China collision; neither is excluded.
steps.quote: one possible regime is the final closure of the Palaeo-Asian Ocean during the Late Triassic

steps.action: The authors read FX-1 and FX-2 as intermediate between the collisional and extensional fields, and link the westward source migration (MDS) to the Early Jurassic transition to extension.
steps.quote: probably representing the transition from the compressional to the extensional setting

steps.action: The authors keep the claim that the Early Jurassic compression-to-extension transition reflects the switch from Palaeo-Asian Ocean closure to Palaeo-Pacific subduction.
steps.quote: The regime was related to the transition from the Palaeo-Asian Ocean's closure to the subduction

steps.action: The authors compare the Cretaceous recycled sources with published subduction and rollback models, fission-track and vitrinite uplift data, and the scarcity of Cretaceous magmatic zircons.
steps.quote: the fission-track analysis (S. Y. Wang et al., 2020) and vitrinite analysis

steps.action: The authors keep the claim that the Cretaceous multiple and recycled sources record high-angle subduction and rollback of the Palaeo-Pacific Plate and the timing of NCC destruction.
steps.quote: our detrital zircon ages add new evidence to the timing of the major period of the NCC destruction

tree.answer: Mesozoic provenance shifts of the northern Ordos Basin
No; inferred from detrital zircon age traces
Establish source-to-sink links and tectonic setting
Five YYOB source areas; for the tectonic driver, two literature regimes
Only LS distinct (770–870 Ma); others overlap, so CDF and MDS were needed
Found: outcrop samples through the stratigraphic column
Partly: MDS agrees with the CDF; unconformities consistent; no resampling or uncertainty
LS excluded; three provenance shifts kept as best explanation

end.claim: The northern Ordos Basin's sources shifted three times in the Mesozoic: YS to JN (Middle Triassic–Early Jurassic), JN to WLS/DQS (Early to latest Middle Jurassic), then multiple and recycled sources in the Early Cretaceous, linked to the shift from Palaeo-Asian closure to Palaeo-Pacific subduction.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the CDF and MDS comparison of the sample age distributions with the published source-area distributions, the provenance shifts could not be distinguished, because the age spectra overlap.

gates.evidence: Action: the samples were collected to 'span the tectonic and sedimentary history' (p. 3252), not directed by a stated hypothesis. Claim: the LS exclusion could have failed (absence of the 770–870 Ma group, p. 3258-3259); the other assignments rest on nearest-neighbour similarity without a stated rejection threshold. Registration: no hypothesis, threshold or analysis was fixed before the data; CDF and MDS were adopted after the spectra comparison failed (p. 3259).

imports.item: Kernel density estimation of age distributions
Multidimensional scaling on Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance matrices
Laser-ablation multicollector ICP mass spectrometry (Neptune Plus LA-ICP-MS)

novelty_claims.quote: This paper also adds new evidence to the basin evolution caused by multiple plate tectonic behaviours in the NCC.
Another important finding was that the northern Ordos Basin's provenance shifted eastwards again during the latest Middle Jurassic
our detrital zircon ages add new evidence to the timing of the major period of the NCC destruction

limits:
No peer-review file was supplied, so the review sequence is not coded. The source-area data are taken from Lei et al. (2017) and are not re-examined.

The MDS is a single unresampled solution, with no uncertainty, although Nordsvan et al. (2020) on resampling is cited. Sample sizes are about 79 grains, and detection limits are not discussed.

The text is internally inconsistent in several places:
- JN is said to have the closest affinity to EM-1, yet YS is concluded (p. 3260).
- 'The Middle Triassic received the resources mostly from the WLS and the DQS' in the Conclusions likely means Middle Jurassic (p. 3264).
- The migration is described as 'eastwards' in §5.2 but 'southward' in the Conclusions.
- The figure references in §4 and §5.1 are mismatched (KDE cited as Figure 3, but shown in Figure 4; source spectra cited as Figure 4b, but shown in Figure 5b).
- The text says 'Middle Triassic' sample, while §3 says 'upper Triassic'.

The tectonic driver rivals (Palaeo-Asian and Mongol-Okhotsk closure versus North–South China collision) are listed but not discriminated. Inference: the tectonic-regime link rests mainly on cited regional evidence and is weaker than the provenance claim.

Sub-claims and their statuses:
- LS excluded as a source: excluded.
- Three dominant age groups: an observation.
- Early Jurassic compression-to-extension transition tied to Palaeo-Pacific subduction: best_explanation, low.
- Cretaceous recycled sources tied to high-angle subduction, rollback and NCC destruction timing: best_explanation, low.

The Cawood CA-DA classification places FX-1 and FX-2 in an 'intermediate zone', which is read as a transition.

disagreements.target: The general practice of constraining provenance by similar peak ages (age-spectra comparison)
disagreements.support: The authors argue that overlapping source-area histograms leave the source ambiguous, and switch to CDF and MDS, which they claim resolve the shifts.
disagreements.quote: leading to continuing uncertainties regarding the actuate source area and the tectonic evolution history

disagreements.target: Previous YYOB-provenance studies (H. Y. Li & Huang 2013; H. Y. Li et al. 2013; Zhou et al. 2019a, b)
disagreements.support: The authors accept the YYOB as the source but state that age-spectra comparison cannot reveal provenance shifts within it; their CDF and MDS analysis yields three shifts.
disagreements.quote: the provenance shifts in the YYOB could not be revealed by comparing the age spectra

alternatives_considered.chosen: Cumulative distribution functions and K-S-based MDS
alternatives_considered.reason: Highly similar age groups in the possible source areas and the northern Ordos Basin

alternatives_considered.chosen: Neither singled out; both listed as possible drivers
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Final closure of the Palaeo-Asian Ocean (and Mongol-Okhotsk Ocean) versus collision between the North and South China blocks
